newsitem.title: FRANCE: No grain export rush despite EU tender move.
newsitem.headline: No grain export rush despite EU tender move.

text.p: The European Union was set to adopt a package of grain export tenders for 1997/98 (July/June) on Thursday -- but officials reiterated this did not mean export subsidies would start flowing as soon as the tenders opened up.
The EU's cereals committee was meeting in Brussels to adopt -- failing an unexpected delay -- at least three new regulations for wheat, barley and rye exports from the domestic market.
Tenders will open on July 17 or July 31, officials said.
European officials have said for weeks that there is no rush to start exporting amid conflicting reports on the new crop, even though most recognise the tender move is a market "signal".
In particular, the Commission appears reluctant to rush into covering a recent one million tonne barley sale to Saudi Arabia at fob prices equating as low as $120 per tonne, officials said.
Saudi Arabia last month bought one million tonnes of optional-origin barley at delivered prices starting at $142 per tonne for arrival in September and October.

Still, officials said there was increasing awareness that potential quality problems from one of the wettest ever months of June could leave the Commission with more feed barley than it had bargained for this year, adding pressure to world prices.
Feed wheat is also seen in big supply this year.
The weather has done little to cut volume expectations for the grain harvest, which according to one official is likely to be "great" in traditional crop areas despite local problems.
"If the weather cooperates slightly, you will have a much better crop than foreseen," the official said. Most estimates are for another large grain crop around 200 million tonnes.
But the current wet weather in much of northwestern Europe weather would have to dry out for several weeks to improve on last year's record crop of some 204-205 million tonnes.
Friday's consultative committee meeting between the European Commission and grain industry in Brussels is being watched for latest grain sowing area, and possibly production, estimates.
Officials said some latest indications were for a grain area increase of a little over 1.5 percent to 37.6 million hectares.

The EU's grain export policy -- strongly moulded by the EU's Austrian Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler -- will remain firmly geared towards domestic price control this year, with affordable internal supplies coming first, officials said.
But EU officials also hinted some increase in the EU's depleted intervention stores of bread-quality wheat would also be seen useful for adjusting to export demand when prices rose.
Last season's 70 percent increase in wheat exports could have been even higher if the EU had been able to respond to a spike in world prices in April with extra supply, one said.

"If we had had three to four million tonne of high quality goods we would not have had to stop exporting," he said. The EU scrapped its previous wheat export tenders in April. --Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
